extracted.intended_audience: Supreme Court justices, patent litigators, patent prosecutors, USPTO examiners, and patent law practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether claimed processes (here, medical/diagnostic/treatment methods) qualify as patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101, and how that threshold inquiry interacts with novelty (§102), nonobviousness (§103), preemption, and related doctrines. Focus is on methods that rely on biological/natural correlations (e.g., metabolite levels) and on drafting/claiming implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 threshold for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 101 marks the threshold of the patent system and 'defines the subject matter that may be patented.' It is a 'coarse filter' to identify categories of statutory subject matter; other Title 35 provisions (e.g., §§102, 103) supply fact-intensive distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three exceptions to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts recognize three specific exceptions to §101's broad terms: 'laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions protect basic tools of science/technology that must remain free for public use. A claim that expressly claims such subjects or in practical effect wholly preempts them is invalid. Apply these exceptions sparingly and with their animating purposes in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process as transformative series of acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'process' is a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result — an act, or series of acts, performed upon the subject-matter to be transformed and reduced to a different state or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transformative nature of a claimed method (e.g., administration of a drug that alters body chemistry, and testing bodily samples) is a classic indicium of §101 eligibility. Consider the claim 'as a whole' rather than dissecting into old and new elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test as a useful clue
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test (tied to a particular machine or transforming an article to a different state or thing) is not the sole test but is a useful and important clue for §101 eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not exclusive, the test is reliable in most cases; courts may consider whether the claimed process is tied to a machine or effects a transformation when evaluating eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformations occurring inside the human body are patent-eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a claimed transformation occurs within the human body does not render the claimed process ineligible; methods of treating patients have long been considered within the field of patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and administrative practice (e.g., many patents with treatment claims, Board decisions like Ex parte Scherer, and precedents such as Diehr and International Tooth Crown) support eligibility for medical treatment methods, subject to other statutory limitations (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 287(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption inquiry — whether claim 'wholly pre-empts' a law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent that in practical effect wholly pre-empts a law of nature, physical phenomenon, or abstract idea is invalid under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the claim would 'preempt all practical applications' of the purported natural law/phenomenon. If substantial opportunities to practice the relationship remain outside the claim, preemption may not exist. Describe the correlation at an appropriate level of generality when assessing preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'laws of nature' that exist independently of human intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Only relationships or correlations that exist apart from human intervention qualify as 'laws of nature' in the relevant sense for §101 exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a correlation arises only by administering synthetic compounds or through human-concocted processes (e.g., metabolite levels present only after administering a synthetic drug), it is not a 'law of nature' for preemption purposes in the same way naturally occurring substances (e.g., homocysteine correlations) are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate §101 eligibility with novelty or inventive contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an invention is novel (§102) or nonobvious (§103) is distinct from whether it falls into a statutory category under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The §101 inquiry should not dissect the claim into old and new elements to test eligibility; novelty and nonobviousness are evaluated under §§102 and 103. A process can be §101-eligible yet invalid under §§102/103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental-step/wherein-clause limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Appending a purely mental step or inference (e.g., a 'wherein' clause that simply instructs interpretation of results or that the result 'indicates a need') to otherwise known physical steps does not, by itself, create a patentable process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the only asserted novelty is a mental inference made after known physical steps, that novelty is unlikely to satisfy §§102/103. Mental steps that do not affect or direct subsequent physical actions add no patentable weight under §101 and are treated skeptically under §§102/103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter doctrine analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of printed matter (e.g., instructions, warnings, labels) added to a known product or process does not impart patentable weight to the product or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By analogy, explicitly stating the medical significance or optimal ranges (e.g., printing a recommended metabolite range on a report or label) would not render a previously known process patentable. The substance of printed instructions is generally irrelevant to patentability when the underlying physical process is unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: When mental steps may be acceptable (decision-tree style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that include mental steps which functionally affect subsequent physical steps (e.g., 'perform A and B, then do either C or D depending on results') can be acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critical distinction is whether the mental step changes what physical acts are to be performed; a mental inference that modifies subsequent physical treatment can be part of a patentable process, whereas a terminal mental 'interpretation' that leaves no further physical action recited generally will not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed numeric ranges and claim scope in preemption analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that specify particular numeric ranges (e.g., metabolite concentrations) may exclude other uses and therefore may not preempt all practical applications of a general correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific numeric limits or explicit exclusions (e.g., excluding transplant patients) narrow claim scope and reduce preemption concerns; whether those limits avoid preemption may depend on whether other practitioners can reasonably rely on substantially different numbers without infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of §§102 and 103 in policing claims that append interpretive steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that append interpretive/mental steps to pre-existing physical processes are properly analyzed under §§102 and 103 for novelty and obviousness rather than rejected under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If administering and assaying steps were known in the prior art, merely adding an interpretive 'wherein' clause identifying a correlation likely fails §§102/103 because it does not recite new physical steps or a new series of acts that differ from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting strategy implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Including concrete downstream treatment steps in claim drafting can help distinguish a claimed process from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants who draft claims to include actionable treatment adjustments (rather than ending with an interpretive mental step) may create more robust novelty/nonobviousness arguments, though doing so may complicate enforcement (proof of attributable steps) and narrow claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining/assaying step as physical manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'determining' step that involves measuring metabolite levels in blood or tissue is a manipulation of a physical substance and is a physical step of the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assaying bodily samples, preparing the sample, and performing measurements are physical acts that contribute to the process's transformative character under §101; nevertheless, if those steps were already known, they may not confer novelty under §§102/103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use §101 as initial coarse filter; reserve factual distinctions for other sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 should be used to identify the types of subject matter that may be eligible; finer-grained factual determinations belong to §§102/103 and other Title 35 provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should avoid using §101 to resolve questions better addressed by §§102/103 (novelty/obviousness) because §101 is designed to be a broad gatekeeper; this maintains predictability and avoids overbroad exclusions of patent-eligible categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption assessment sensitive to level of generality
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which a claim preempts a natural relationship depends on how the relationship is characterized—very fine particularity vs. high-level generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a correlation is described at a very fine degree of particularity (e.g., specific metabolite thresholds), preemption arguments may be stronger; if described at higher generality, many practical uses may remain available. Courts should beware of describing inventions at such a general level that every invention would appear to 'claim' a correlation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement proof requires attribution of every claimed step
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability for infringing a process patent generally requires proof that every step of the infringing conduct was attributable to the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because infringement of a process claim under 35 U.S.C. 271(a) demands that all steps be performed by or attributable to the accused infringer, adding treatment steps may make enforcement harder against third parties who only perform some steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative precedents to apply in §101 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Key Supreme Court precedents shaping §101 include Diamond v. Chakrabarty, Gottschalk v. Benson, Diamond v. Diehr, Funk Bros., Parker v. Flook, Bilski v. Kappos, LabCorp (Breyer opinion), and related Federal Circuit decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these precedents to distinguish (a) claims that expressly claim laws of nature or abstract ideas, (b) claims that merely append mental steps to known processes, and (c) claims that recite transformative, concrete processes. Apply precedents consistently and recall that some tests (e.g., machine-or-transformation) are helpful clues but not exclusive rules.
